title: Use population data

blocks.heading: Use population data
blocks.text: Population data can guide the location and capacity of services, employment planning and infrastructure. For a Namibian planning application, compare district age groups and access to schools or clinics rather than distributing capacity solely by national totals. Use the date and local denominators.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Economic uses
blocks.text: Age and location data can inform workforce training, transport demand and markets. Counts of working-age residents do not directly measure available skills or job seekers; combine population structure with relevant labour information.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Social uses
blocks.text: Children’s and older residents’ counts can inform school, health and care planning. Needs depend on location and actual access as well as age. A distant facility may offer less usable capacity than its place count suggests.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Apply the measure
blocks.text: Describe this fictional planning comparison: A has 400 school-age children and 200 places; B has 200 children and 200 places. A has a 200-place shortfall while B’s recorded capacity matches its count. Equal place allocation therefore corresponds to unequal coverage.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect population evidence to Health (7.2), Education (7.3) and Urbanisation (4.2). Check dates, boundaries, denominators and units before explaining what a pattern supports.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
